items.summary: The `aria-describedby` technique solves the problem of providing detailed, contextual information to users about a specific user interface control that cannot be included directly in the visible label. It allows developers to programmatically associate descriptive text or instructions with an element. To implement this, you apply the `aria-describedby` attribute to the control and reference the target elements using their unique `id` attributes. This ensures that assistive technologies can read the associated descriptions when a user interacts with the control. This technique relates primarily to Success Criteria 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) and 3.3.2 (Labels or Instructions).

items.summary: The `aria-labelledby` technique solves the problem of providing a meaningful text alternative for elements that lack sufficient visible labels, particularly complex graphics or non-text content. It allows developers to associate an element with descriptive text located elsewhere on the page using unique `id` attributes. To implement this, you apply the `aria-labelledby` attribute to the element and set its value to the `id` of the labeling element. This ensures that assistive technologies, such as screen readers, can read the associated text and understand the purpose or description of the element. This technique directly supports WCAG Success Criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content).

items.summary: This technique uses ARIA landmarks to provide programmatic access to distinct regions of a web page, solving the problem of inefficient navigation for users relying on assistive technologies or keyboard-only input. Landmarks help users orient themselves by allowing them to quickly jump between major sections, such as main content or navigation menus, effectively acting like "skip links." Implementation involves applying specific landmark roles (like `main`, `navigation`, or `banner`) to HTML elements that define these structural areas. This approach improves accessibility by giving users a clear understanding of the page's structure and allowing them to bypass repetitive content easily. The technique relates primarily to WCAG Success Criteria 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships), 1.3.6 (Identify Purpose), and 2.4.1 (Bypass Blocks).

items.summary: This technique addresses the need for Assistive Technologies (AT) to correctly identify content as a heading, especially when native HTML heading elements are not used. To implement this, developers apply `role="heading"` to an element and pair it with the `aria-level` property to define its hierarchical level. It is strongly recommended to use native HTML heading elements (`<h1>` through `<h6>`) instead of custom `div`s with ARIA roles, as native elements provide necessary implicit styling and functionality. While this method allows for defining non-standard heading levels (like level 7), caution should be exercised regarding very high `aria-level` values to avoid user confusion. This technique relates directly to the WAI-ARIA specifications and the semantic requirements of HTML structure.

items.summary: The `aria-labelledby` technique solves the problem of providing meaningful, programmatic names for specific regions or landmarks on a webpage so that assistive technologies can accurately inform users about the page structure. It allows developers to associate a section marked with a landmark role (like `complementary` or `application`) with descriptive text found elsewhere on the page. To implement this, you apply `aria-labelledby` to the region and provide the `id` of an element that contains the desired label. This ensures that screen readers can read the associated text and understand the context of the landmark. The technique relates directly to ARIA principles for defining structure and relationships within web content.

items.summary: The `aria-label` technique solves the problem of providing a clear, accessible name for elements when visible text labels are unavailable or insufficient. This is crucial for users relying on assistive technologies who need to understand the purpose of interactive components, such as icons or custom controls. To implement this, you apply the `aria-label` attribute directly to an element to define its accessible name (e.g., setting `aria-label="Close"` on a button). This ensures that screen readers accurately communicate the function of the control to all users. The technique relates primarily to WCAG Success Criterion 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A), ensuring that all user interface components are properly labeled.

items.summary: The `aria-describedby` technique solves the problem of providing detailed descriptions for images when the short alternative text (`alt` attribute) is insufficient to convey the image's full function or information. This feature allows developers to associate long, descriptive text with an image by linking it to a separate element using unique `id` attributes. To implement this, you apply `aria-describedby` to the image and list the corresponding `id` of the descriptive text in the attribute's value. This method ensures that comprehensive descriptions are available to all users, including those using assistive technologies. It relates primarily to WAI-ARIA principles for enhancing non-text content accessibility.

items.summary: The `aria-labelledby` technique solves the problem of providing meaningful, accessible names for user interface controls when dedicated visible labels are unavailable or context is more appropriate. It allows developers to associate a control, such as an input field, with one or more text elements elsewhere on the page using their IDs. To implement this, you apply the `aria-labelledby` attribute to the control, providing a space-separated list of the IDs of the elements that serve as its labels. This technique is crucial for ensuring that assistive technologies can accurately announce the purpose of interactive elements. It relates directly to Success Criteria 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A) and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A).

items.summary: This technique addresses the need to programmatically group related form controls when standard HTML elements like `fieldset` are impractical due to design constraints. It allows assistive technologies to understand that a set of inputs belongs together, providing a common label or qualifier for the entire group. Implementation involves applying either `role="group"` or, specifically for radio buttons, `role="radiogroup"` to the container element. Crucially, this grouping must be linked to an accessible name using `aria-labelledby` to provide context to screen reader users. This method is a viable alternative for structuring complex form layouts where visual grouping is insufficient.

items.summary: This technique addresses the need to effectively communicate input errors to users in a clear, modal manner. It solves the problem of ensuring that critical feedback regarding invalid data is immediately visible and actionable. Implementation involves using `role="alertdialog"` to define the notification, ensuring it functions as a modal window with proper focus management (focus moves into the dialog and remains constrained while open). Crucially, developers must use attributes like `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` to provide an accessible name for the alert. This pattern relates primarily to Success Criteria 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 3.3.3 (Error Suggestion), as well as 4.1.3 (Status Messages).

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of ensuring that users relying on Assistive Technologies (AT), such as screen readers, are immediately notified when input errors occur on a form. It allows dynamic error messages to be announced automatically without requiring the user to manually navigate to the error location. Implementation involves marking an error container with `role=alert` or `aria-live` and using JavaScript to inject error messages into that container upon submission failure. This setup ensures that ATs automatically read and announce the newly injected content, providing crucial feedback about validation issues. It relates primarily to WCAG Success Criteria 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 4.1.3 (Status Messages).

items.summary: The `aria-required` technique solves the problem of ensuring that form fields which are visually marked as mandatory are also programmatically identifiable as required by assistive technologies. This property provides an explicit, machine-readable indication that user input is necessary before a form can be successfully submitted. To implement this, developers set the attribute to `aria-required="true"` on the relevant input element. It is most effective when used alongside visual indicators, such as asterisks or specific styling, to provide comprehensive information to all users. This technique relates primarily to WCAG Success Criterion 3.3.2 (Labels or Instructions) and 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships).

items.summary: The `role="region"` technique solves the problem of identifying significant, self-contained sections of content on a page that do not fit standard document landmark roles. It allows user agents and assistive technologies to programmatically recognize these segments as distinct areas for navigation and discovery. To implement this, you apply `role="region"` to the container element and provide a programmatic name using attributes like `aria-labelledby` or `aria-label`. This ensures that users can easily understand the scope of the content within the region. The technique relates directly to ARIA principles concerning structure and relationships (A).

items.summary: This technique addresses the need for accessible error identification, ensuring that users are notified when they submit invalid data or fail validation within a form. It solves the problem of making validation failures discoverable by assistive technologies, which is crucial for meeting accessibility standards. To implement it, set the `aria-invalid` attribute to `"true"` on an input field whenever its content fails validation. This state should be paired with clear, descriptive error messages or associated instructions (using attributes like `aria-describedby`) so that screen reader users understand the nature of the error. This practice directly supports WCAG success criterion 3.3.1 Error Identification by clearly communicating the status and nature of input errors.

items.summary: This technique addresses the accessibility challenge where font icons, often implemented using icon fonts, disappear when users override the `font-family` via CSS, making them invisible to low-vision users. It solves this by providing a semantic way to differentiate between standard text and meaningful visual icons. Implementation involves marking the icon element with `role="img"` and then using CSS selectors, such as `*:not([role="img"])`, to selectively exclude these elements from font family overrides. This ensures that the icon fonts remain visible while allowing general text styling to be applied elsewhere on the page. The technique primarily relates to ARIA principles (Info and Relationships) and CSS specificity.

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of dynamically updating status information, such as a progress bar, which may not be automatically announced by assistive technologies. It ensures that changes in the state of an element are communicated effectively to users relying on screen readers. To implement this, you should use an `aria-live` region (like `aria-live="polite"`) for the status message that updates with the progress. This allows assistive technologies to announce the dynamic changes made to the content. The technique relates primarily to making dynamic content accessible and aligns with the requirements of Success Criterion 4.1.3 Status Messages.

items.summary: The `aria-current` technique solves the problem of programmatically indicating the current item within a set of related elements in a user interface. It allows assistive technologies to inform users which item is currently active or selected, even if that status is only visually highlighted. To implement this, you apply the `aria-current` attribute to the element that represents the current state, using specific values such as `page`, `step`, or `time`. This technique directly supports WCAG success criteria 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) and 2.4.8 (Location). By using this attribute, you ensure that the context of navigation, process steps, or schedules is clearly communicated to users relying on screen readers.

items.summary: This technique addresses the challenge of communicating dynamic status updates, such as file upload progress, to assistive technologies. It allows developers to programmatically announce changes in a progress bar to screen reader users, ensuring they are aware of the ongoing process. Implementation involves updating the visual progress bar and then calling the `ariaNotify` method with the relevant status text via JavaScript. While experimental, this method provides an ARIA-based way to convey status messages, serving as a progressive enhancement for dynamic content updates. It relates primarily to ARIA principles for conveying state and status (specifically related to 4.1.3 Status Messages).

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of making complex or custom user interface components understandable to assistive technologies by providing semantic meaning beyond standard HTML elements. It allows developers to define the specific function and relationship of an element using predefined WAI-ARIA roles, such as `toolbar` or `treeitem`. Implementation involves applying a non-abstract role value to the relevant HTML element, ensuring that the role accurately describes the component's characteristics. By correctly defining these roles, users and screen readers gain a clear understanding of how to interact with the widget. This technique directly supports WCAG Success Criterion 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) by ensuring that the accessible name and role of the component are properly communicated.

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of making dynamic user interface components accessible to assistive technologies by exposing their current state, properties, and values. It allows screen readers and other AT to understand how a widget functions and how a user can interact with it. Implementation involves applying specific WAI-ARIA state and property attributes—such as `aria-pressed` for toggles or `aria-valuenow` for sliders—to the relevant HTML elements. This ensures that changes in the component's status are communicated to assistive technology, fulfilling accessibility requirements related to dynamic content. While this technique relies on standard HTML structure, it is fundamentally an ARIA guideline

It allows developers to explicitly define what an element represents, ensuring screen reader users understand the purpose of interactive components or structural regions. Authors must remember that `aria-label` overrides native naming (like `alt` or `label`) and should be used in conjunction with other ARIA properties when necessary for accurate accessibility.

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of providing clear, unambiguous context for links, especially when the visible link text alone is insufficient for screen reader users. It allows authors to associate a link with descriptive text elements elsewhere on the page, ensuring that the link's purpose is fully understood. To implement this, you assign unique `id`s to relevant text elements and use the `aria-labelledby` attribute on the link, referencing these IDs in the attribute's value. The screen reader then announces the concatenated text of these referenced labels instead of just the link text. This method is crucial for creating meaningful accessible names that enhance navigation and comprehension according to WCAG principles.

items.summary: This technique addresses the need to clearly communicate the purpose of a link to users, especially when the visible link text is insufficient or repetitive. It solves the problem of ensuring that assistive technologies can accurately convey the context and destination of a link, allowing users to distinguish between various destinations. To implement this, you should use the `aria-label` attribute on an anchor element (`<a>`) to provide a descriptive label that overrides the visible link text. For consistency, it is recommended to start the `aria-label` with the existing link text. This practice supports accessibility requirements such as SC 2.4.4 and 2.4.9 regarding link purpose, and SC 2.5.3 Label in Name.

items.summary: The `aria-labelledby` technique solves the problem of providing a comprehensive and meaningful accessible name for input elements when that name must be constructed from multiple separate text strings. This is particularly useful in complex contexts, such as nesting an input within a full sentence or creating labels for table headers where visible space is limited. To implement it, you assign unique `id`s to the individual label strings and then set the `aria-labelledby` attribute on the input element with a space-separated list of those IDs. Screen readers will concatenate these referenced labels to form a single, descriptive name for the input. This technique supports success criteria related to providing accessible names (1.1.1) and proper labeling (3.3.2).

items.summary: This technique addresses accessibility concerns by ensuring text content is proportionally scalable for all users. The problem it solves is allowing users to effectively scale text sizes without breaking the layout or requiring manual adjustments. To implement this, developers should use percentage values when setting the `font-size` property in CSS, rather than fixed units like pixels. This approach allows user agents and assistive technologies to scale the content appropriately based on user preferences. It relates directly to CSS properties governing typography and inheritance, specifically the `font-size` property.

items.summary: This technique addresses the need for flexible and relative text resizing that respects user preferences and accessibility standards. Instead of using fixed pixel values, it allows developers to specify font sizes using predefined keywords like `smaller`, `larger`, or `medium`. This approach provides hints to the user agent, enabling it to adjust the actual font size based on the user's settings. By implementing named font sizes, content becomes more adaptable for users who require different text scales. The technique relates directly to the CSS `font-size` property and its associated scaling mechanisms.

items.summary: This technique addresses the need for providing clear visual feedback to users regarding interactive elements on a webpage. It solves the problem of making it obvious which component is currently selected or actionable by highlighting its state when focused or hovered over. Implementation involves using CSS pseudo-classes, such as `:focus`, `:hover`, and `:focus-visible`, applied to HTML elements. By applying these styles, developers can enhance usability and accessibility, ensuring users know the scope of interactive areas. This technique directly relates to CSS selectors that target element states.

items.summary: This technique addresses the issue of ensuring that text within form controls remains readable and scalable for all users. It solves the problem where changing the base font size in the user agent does not proportionally affect the size of input fields or labels, leading to poor usability. To implement this, developers should use relative CSS units, such as `em` or `rem`, when setting font sizes for form elements and their associated text. This ensures that all related components scale together consistently. The technique primarily relates to typography and layout properties, specifically the `font-size` property in CSS.

items.summary: This technique addresses the outdated practice of using spacer images (like 1x1 transparent GIFs) for controlling layout spacing in web design. It solves the problem by providing a modern, flexible method to manage element spacing directly through CSS. To implement this, designers should use the `margin` properties to control the space outside an element and the `padding` properties to control the space inside an element. These properties can be applied to any block-level or general element to precisely define layout dimensions. This concept is fundamentally related to the CSS Box Model, specifically the margin and padding components defined in the CSS Box Model Module Level 3 specification.

items.summary:
This technique addresses readability issues for users with cognitive disabilities who struggle to track lines of text when content is single-spaced. By increasing the line spacing, it provides necessary visual separation between lines, making it easier for these users to start a new line and process the text effectively. To implement this, you use the CSS `line-height` property on the desired element, setting a value typically between 1.5 and 2.
For example, setting `line-height: 1.5;` in the style sheet adjusts the vertical space of the text. This practice relates to accessibility standards, specifically WCAG criteria 1.4.12 Text Spacing (AA) and 1.4.8 Visual Presentation (AAA).

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of allowing users to customize the colors of the main content while maintaining visual organization and grouping on a webpage. It achieves this by specifying text and background colors only for secondary elements, such as navigation bars or banners, leaving the main content's colors undefined. This allows the browser to use the user agent's default color preferences for the primary content, ensuring optimal readability for the user. Implementation involves applying specific CSS styles to these secondary sections without defining foreground or background colors for the main area. This technique is related to general visual presentation and color management within CSS.

It solves the problem of content overflow by allowing text to reflow naturally within the browser window. To implement this, developers should specify the width of CSS containers using percentage values rather than fixed units. This method ensures that the layout remains responsive and readable regardless of the user's text size settings. The technique primarily relates to CSS layout and visual presentation standards.

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of ensuring structural layout and visual delineation remain intact, regardless of user-defined text and background colors. It prevents display conflicts where browser settings override author-specified borders or layout arrangements, which is particularly important for accessibility. To implement this, developers specify CSS properties related to borders and layout (like `border`, `float`, or `display`) while intentionally omitting any color declarations for text or backgrounds. This separation allows users to apply their preferred visual themes without disrupting the intended page structure. The technique relies on standard CSS layout and border properties

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of ensuring that the logical order of content in the source code matches its visual presentation on the screen. Mismatches can confuse users relying on assistive technologies, such as screen readers or keyboard navigation, by presenting information in an illogical sequence. To implement this effectively, developers must structure the HTML so that the DOM order aligns with the visual flow of the page. While CSS is used to control visual layout, the primary fix involves careful structuring of the HTML elements themselves. This technique relates primarily to WCAG Success Criterion 1.3.2 (Meaningful Sequence) and 2.4.3 (Focus Order).

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of ensuring that text containers and form controls remain properly sized when users adjust their system text size settings. By using `em` units to define the width and height of these containers, the layout scales proportionally with the font size, preventing text cropping or overflow. To implement this, apply `em` units to the dimensions of any container that holds text or accepts input, such as `div`s, `input` elements, or `select` boxes. This ensures that interactive elements and content remain accessible and visible regardless of the user's accessibility preferences. The technique relates directly to CSS specifications concerning text spacing and text resizing (1.4.12 and 1.4.4).

items.summary: This technique demonstrates how CSS and scripting can be used to replace structured text with images of that text, allowing users to choose their preferred presentation. The primary goal is to provide an alternative view for content, addressing accessibility requirements related to presenting text visually. Implementation involves creating two separate stylesheets—one showing plain text and one using CSS image replacement—and using a control (scripting) to switch between these views. This method helps authors meet Success Criteria 1.4.5 Images of Text or 1.4.9 Images of Text by offering an alternate presentation. It is crucial that the switching control is easily accessible and ensures that the resulting page includes the text programmatically determined, regardless of the visual format.

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of content overflow by allowing text and elements to reflow dynamically within the available viewport space, thereby eliminating unnecessary horizontal or vertical scroll bars. It achieves this by utilizing CSS Flexbox layouts, which define layout regions that adapt their size based on the screen dimensions and zoom levels. Implementation involves setting a container to `display: flex` with properties like `flex-flow: row wrap` and using `flex-basis` combined with media queries to control how items wrap or resize. This method ensures content remains fully accessible without requiring scrolling, improving readability across different devices and zoom preferences. The technique relates primarily to the CSS Flexible Box Layout module and the general concept of reflow (AA).

items.summary: This technique addresses the issue where long strings of text, such as URLs, can cause horizontal or vertical scrollbars when the page is zoomed, breaking the reflow behavior. To solve this, the method uses CSS properties to force long words to break and wrap appropriately within their containers. Implementation involves applying `overflow-wrap: break-word` and `word-wrap: break-word` to the relevant HTML elements containing the long text. These properties ensure that content adapts to the available viewport space without introducing unwanted scrollbars, improving accessibility and usability for long content.

items.summary: This technique addresses the issue of sticky headers and footers that can consume excessive screen space, particularly on mobile devices in landscape orientation or when users zoom in. It solves this by dynamically adjusting the fixed positioning of these elements to allow for more available content space. Implementation involves using CSS media queries—specifically `min-height`, `max-height`, and `min-width`—to conditionally un-fix or adjust the boundaries of sticky regions based on the viewport size and orientation. This adjustment improves readability and usability, especially for users in landscape mode, while also mitigating accessibility issues related to keyboard navigation. This technique relates directly to Success Criterion 1.4.10 Reflow (AA).

items.summary: This technique addresses the need for users to override default text spacing (line height, word spacing) via user stylesheets, improving readability for people with low vision or cognitive disabilities. To implement this, authors must ensure that containers containing text are sized appropriately or configured to expand when text spacing is applied, preventing content truncation or overlap. If fixed widths are necessary, containers should be set wider than the default text width (e.g., 20% wider). Alternatively, using CSS properties like `display: inline-block` allows elements to expand naturally with the text, enabling flexible spacing adjustments without breaking layout functionality. This technique primarily relates to CSS display properties and width management.

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of images overflowing their containers, which can introduce unwanted horizontal or vertical scrollbars in responsive layouts. Implementation is achieved by defining `max-width` for images (typically setting it to 100%) so they adapt to the available space. This ensures that content remains visible and fits within the viewport, even when zoom levels are increased. The technique relies on CSS sizing properties like `max-width` and `height` to manage image dimensions effectively in dynamic environments.

items.summary: This technique addresses the need to prevent motion animations from causing distraction or discomfort for users who prefer reduced motion. It allows users to signal their preference for less motion through system settings, enabling websites to adapt their visual experience accordingly. Implementation involves using the CSS `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` query to conditionally disable or modify CSS animations when the user has requested a reduced motion setting. This method ensures that motion effects are suppressed for users who experience vestibular disorders or sensitivity to movement. It directly relates to WCAG success criterion 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions.

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of ensuring focus indicators have sufficient contrast against diverse background colors, which is often difficult when using a single color. It achieves this by creating a two-color indicator—a light and a dark shade—that guarantees at least one color will pass the required 3:1 contrast ratio against any solid background. Implementation involves combining the `outline` and `box-shadow` properties with `:focus` or `:focus-visible` pseudo-classes. Authors must ensure the two colors themselves have a high contrast ratio (at least 9:1) to guarantee compatibility across various backgrounds. This technique relates primarily to WCAG success criteria 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast), 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance), and 2.4.7 (Focus Visible).

It is crucial to ensure this indicator is large enough (at least 2 CSS pixels) and maintains a high contrast ratio (at least 3:1) with the surrounding area. This technique relates directly to the use of the `:focus` pseudo-class and related CSS properties for improving focus appearance.

items.summary: This technique addresses the need for sufficient target size and spacing in navigation menus, ensuring that links in pagination or navigation are clearly separated. The primary problem solved is preventing accidental activation of adjacent links by providing adequate clearance for pointer input. To implement this, apply `min-height` and `min-width` (e.g., 24px) to the container elements (such as list items) that hold the interactive targets. This forces the containers to occupy a minimum area, guaranteeing sufficient space between links. The technique relates primarily to CSS layout properties like `min-height`, `min-width`, and potentially flexbox or margin settings used for spacing.

It ensures that content underneath these fixed overlays remains accessible and visible when a user navigates using the Tab key or other focus methods. Implementation involves applying CSS `padding` and specifically the `scroll-padding` property to the container element that is scrolling, calculating the necessary space based on the height of the obscuring fixed component. This method creates necessary visual breathing room, preventing content from being hidden beneath fixed elements. The technique relates directly to the CSS properties `padding` and the newer `scroll-padding`.

It allows developers to distinguish between focus received via keyboard navigation and focus received via mouse interaction. To implement this, you apply custom styles using the CSS `:focus-visible` pseudo-class instead of the standard `:focus`. User agents automatically handle the logic, showing these styles primarily when a user is navigating with the keyboard. This method ensures that keyboard focus indicators are prominent for keyboard users while maintaining flexibility for other interaction methods.

The primary problem solved is ensuring that visual enhancements do not compromise the structural integrity or accessibility of the content, especially when stylesheets are disabled. Implementation involves applying absolute positioning properties, such as `position: absolute` along with `left` and `top` values, to specific elements to control their display location on the viewport. This method relies on existing structural markup (like definition lists) to maintain the logical reading order and meaning of the content. The technique relates directly to CSS positioning properties, specifically `position`, `top`, `left`, and `margin`.

It allows web authors to supplement truncated link text with descriptive information that is accessible to assistive technologies like screen readers. items.summary: This technique addresses the failure condition where combining multiple content formats or plug-ins traps the user's keyboard focus. The core problem is that certain plug-ins can lock the keyboard focus within their content, preventing users from navigating outside of it. To implement this test, one must check if the keyboard focus can be moved out of the trapped content without closing the plug-in or restarting the system. This failure condition relates directly to Success Criterion 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap) and Conformance Requirement 5.

items.summary: This technique describes a failure in adhering to Success Criterion 1.3.4 Orientation, specifically when content is partially hidden or blocked based on device orientation rather than being fully reoriented. The problem arises when an author displays a message asking the user to rotate their device instead of ensuring the entire content adapts to the new orientation. To implement this failure, developers use CSS media queries targeting the `orientation` property to conditionally hide or display elements (like content or messages). This technique highlights that detecting orientation is not the issue; the failure occurs when the author fails to reorient all author-controlled content as required by the criterion.

items.summary: This technique describes a failure scenario where interactive controls execute functionality immediately upon a pointer press (the `down-event`) rather than waiting for release. The problem arises when this execution is not reversible or intended, potentially leading to accidental actions or data loss for the user. To implement this failure, developers must trigger critical functionality using events like `mousedown` or `touchstart`, ensuring that the outcome does not reverse upon the subsequent `up-event`. This failure relates directly to Success Criterion 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation (A), which requires that pointer interactions are cancellable and reversible.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure where content disappears or becomes inaccessible when the viewport reflows, specifically when narrowing the screen width (e.g., to 320px). The problem arises because content available at wider viewports is not properly presented in a single-column layout, leading to loss of information. To solve this, developers must ensure that all essential content remains accessible after the reflow, even if it is repositioned or hidden. Implementation requires using disclosure widgets, dialogs, or links to provide alternative access paths for the missing information. This failure relates directly to Success Criterion 1.4.10 Reflow, ensuring that content availability is maintained regardless of viewport size changes.

items.summary: This technique addresses failures where dynamic status messages are present in content but fail to be communicated to users via assistive technologies. It helps developers identify when information about application state, progress, or errors is displayed without using appropriate WAI-ARIA roles or properties. To implement this test, check if dynamically added content meets the definition of a status message (e.g., providing results or error states) and verify that its container lacks necessary ARIA attributes like `role="status"` or an `aria-live` setting. The failure occurs if the status message exists but is not surfaced by assistive technology. This technique relates directly to Success Criterion 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA).

items.summary: This technique addresses failures where text content becomes clipped or overlapped when mandated text spacing rules are applied. It identifies issues where size constraints prevent the content from expanding to accommodate increased line height, paragraph spacing, or letter/word spacing. To implement this test, check if the content remains fully visible and correctly positioned after applying the required CSS text spacing overrides. This failure occurs typically when elements use properties like `overflow: hidden` or fixed borders that do not expand dynamically with the new spacing requirements. The technique relates directly to Success Criterion 1.4.12 regarding Text Spacing (AA).

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure of Success Criterion 2.5.1 by ensuring that functionality operated via complex path-based pointer gestures has simple, accessible alternatives. The core problem is that if a feature relies solely on drawing or swiping paths to perform an action, users who cannot perform these gestures (such as those using assistive technologies or devices without gesture support) are excluded. To implement this failure, content must provide alternative methods—like taps or clicks—to achieve the same result as the path-based gesture. This ensures that all pointer users have a viable way to interact with controls, regardless of their input method. It relates directly to Success Criterion 2.5.1 (Pointer Gestures).

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure condition where motion actuation cannot be deactivated, which is critical for users with motor impairments or tremors who may accidentally trigger functions via shaking or tilting. The core problem solved is ensuring that motion-based input mechanisms are controllable and prevent unintended activation. To implement this successfully, developers must provide a mechanism (like a setting) to disable motion detection whenever it is not essential for the function's operation. This failure relates directly to the success criterion 2.5.4 Motion Actuation (A). It is closely related to technique G213, which advocates for providing conventional controls and application settings for motion-activated input.

It solves the problem of ensuring that form fields accurately communicate their intended purpose to assistive technologies and machine processing systems. To implement this, testers must check if the values assigned to the `autocomplete` attribute match the actual information requested by the input (e.g., using `name` for a name field). The procedure involves verifying that the input purpose is not communicated through other means. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 1.3.5, which requires identifying the purpose of user interface components.

items.summary: This technique addresses a failure where functionality is only accessible through dragging movements, which creates an accessibility barrier for users with motor impairments. The core problem solved is ensuring that functions can be actuated using a single pointer input method, rather than mandating a drag-and-drop action. To implement this successfully, developers must provide an alternative way to perform the required action—such as activating elements or selecting drop destinations—that does not rely on dragging. This failure condition specifically relates to Success Criterion 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA). It mandates that if a function involves moving targets, there must be a non-dragging, single pointer input alternative available for operation.

items.summary: This technique addresses failures in accessible authentication by ensuring users can enter passwords or codes in their original format. The core problem is that requiring users to input individual characters or digits across multiple fields prevents them from using standard efficiency tools like password managers or pasting, forcing unnecessary transcription and creating a cognitive burden. To implement this correctly, all input fields accepting sensitive information must allow the user to enter the entire password or code in the same format it was originally created. This ensures that authentication processes are accessible and do not rely on non-standard cognitive functions. The technique relates directly to Success Criteria 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication Minimum) and 3.3.9 (Accessible Authentication Enhanced).

The core problem is that these fixed elements can hide interactive controls that a user attempts to tab to, violating the principle of focus visibility. To implement this fix, developers must ensure that sticky content does not overlap or cover any element currently in focus during scrolling. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), ensuring that keyboard navigation remains fully accessible regardless of the viewport position.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure of providing necessary audio descriptions for important visual content in synchronized media. The core problem is the omission of audio descriptions during natural pauses in dialogue when crucial visual information is being conveyed. To implement this, creators must use these dialogue pauses to insert audio descriptions of important actions, scene changes, or on-screen text. It is essential that these pauses are long enough and contextually appropriate for the visual content being described. This technique directly relates to ensuring compliance with Success Criterion 1.2.5 regarding audio description requirements.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure of session management systems to persist user input when a session times out and the user must re-authenticate. The core problem is that if the system does not save previously entered data, users are forced to restart complex tasks after logging back in, which can lead to an impossible experience. To implement this correctly, web applications must ensure that all user inputs collected during an authenticated session are securely saved and restored upon re-authentication. This ensures continuity for users who require more time to complete forms or processes. It relates directly to Success Criterion 2.2.5 regarding the proper handling of re-authentication and session state restoration.

The problem it solves is ensuring accessibility for users with color vision deficiencies or those who rely on text descriptions, preventing them from missing critical data presented visually. To implement this correctly, ensure that any information conveyed by color—such as status, quantity, or categorization—is explicitly described in the image's text alternative. This failure condition relates directly to Success Criteria 1.1.1 (Non-text Content) and 1.4.1 (Use of Color).

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure that occurs when custom user interface controls are implemented without properly exposing their properties to the platform's accessibility API. The core problem is that assistive technologies cannot understand what a custom control is or how to operate it if the necessary information is missing. To implement this fix, developers must ensure that all custom controls correctly expose their roles, names, values, and states using the appropriate accessibility APIs, often leveraging WAI-ARIA standards. This ensures that custom components are fully accessible to users relying on assistive technologies. It directly relates to Success Criterion 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value).

It ensures that window creation is intentional and controlled by the user interaction. To implement this, testers must check if clicking links or elements results in a new window without explicit user request. This control must operate independently of the overall system volume settings. This failure directly relates to Success Criterion 1.4.2 Audio Control (A), which mandates proper management and control over audio output.

The core problem is that without alternative text, screen readers cannot convey the purpose or content of an image. To implement this correctly, developers must provide a descriptive `alt` attribute for all `img`, `area`, and `input type="image"` elements. If providing simple text is insufficient, appropriate WAI-ARIA attributes like `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` can be used, provided they are accessibility supported. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 1.1.1 Non-text Content (A).

To implement this correctly, developers must ensure that any repeated navigation mechanism always presents its links in the exact same sequence on every page. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 3.2.3 (Consistent Navigation), requiring all navigational elements to maintain a predictable order across the site.

items.summary: This technique addresses failures where form controls lack a programmatically determined name accessible to assistive technologies, preventing users from understanding the purpose of the control. The core problem is that visual labels are not properly associated with their corresponding input fields, making the form inaccessible to screen reader users. To implement this correctly, developers must use explicit associations, primarily by linking `<label>` elements to inputs using the `for` and `id` attributes. items.summary: This technique addresses failures in how web content handles text resizing, specifically ensuring that layout containers do not clip or obscure content when text expands significantly. The problem occurs when a user agent's layout engine fails to correctly honor font size hints, leading to visual artifacts like truncated or hidden text. To test this failure, increase the text size by 200% and verify that no text, images, or controls are clipped or obscured within their containers. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 1.4.4, which mandates that text should be properly resizable without losing content visibility.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure of content that blinks within plug-ins or applets without providing a mechanism for pausing the animation. The problem arises when blinking content is too fast or continuous, preventing users from reading the information or avoiding distraction. To implement this check, testers must determine if the blinking content continues for more than five seconds and whether there is any available method (via user agent settings or plugin controls) to pause the blinking. If content blinks excessively without a pause option, it fails the success criterion related to pausing dynamic content. This technique relates directly to Success Criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A).

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure to provide accessible alternatives for non-text content, specifically ASCII art. The problem solved is ensuring that visual information conveyed by ASCII art is perceivable and understandable to users who rely on assistive technologies, such as screen readers. To implement this correctly, whenever ASCII art is used to convey meaning (rather than just being decorative), a text alternative must be provided nearby. items.summary: This technique addresses failures in making interactive elements, such as links, distinguishable from surrounding content for users with color vision deficiencies. The core problem is relying solely on color differences (hue) to indicate interactivity, which fails accessibility standards when color is the only distinguishing feature. To implement this correctly, ensure that all links are visually identifiable through non-color cues, such as underlining, bolding, or sufficient contrast differences. If a link's distinction relies only on color, it must also have an alternative visual indicator to be accessible. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color (A).

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure of not properly labeling synchronized media alternatives when they substitute for text. The core problem is that users cannot easily find these enhanced media formats because they are not clearly linked to the specific text they replace. To implement this fix, ensure that any synchronized media provided as an alternative to text is explicitly labeled with the exact text it substitutes. This ensures that users who rely on text alternatives and those seeking synchronized media can locate the correct content efficiently. This failure condition relates directly to Success Criteria 1.2.2 (Captions) and 1.2.8 (Media Alternative).

This failure condition relates directly to Success Criteria 1.2.2 (Captions), 1.2.3 (Audio Description or Media Alternative), and 1.2.5 (Audio Description).

items.summary: This technique addresses failures where a user interface component's focus state is not programmatically determinable or when changes in focus are not communicated to assistive technologies. The problem is that without this information, screen readers and other assistive tools cannot accurately inform users which element currently has focus, leading to confusion and poor accessibility. To resolve this failure, developers must ensure custom UI components use appropriate accessibility APIs to expose the focus state. Furthermore, they must implement mechanisms to notify assistive technologies whenever the focus moves between different components. This ensures that all users, regardless of their interaction method, have a clear understanding of the current context within the interface.

items.summary: This technique addresses failures where captions do not accurately represent the full content of the material. The core problem is that captions may omit essential dialogue or important sound effects, meaning they are not true representations of the audio stream. To implement this correctly, ensure that all spoken dialogue and all significant sounds are included in the captioning process. While captions can simplify text for readability, they must never exclude critical information. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 1.2.2 concerning the accuracy and completeness of prerecorded captions.

items.summary: This failure condition addresses the issue where text-based form controls fail to resize when the user changes the overall visual text size. The problem is that if the surrounding text is scaled up, interactive elements like input boxes and textareas do not scale proportionally, making them difficult or impossible for users to interact with and read accurately. To implement this test, one must increase the font size of the content by 200% and verify that the form controls maintain the correct proportional scaling. This technique directly relates to Success Criterion 1.4.4, ensuring that text-based form controls are scalable and accessible across different text sizes.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure condition where required fields or error states are identified solely by color differences, which violates accessibility standards for users with color vision deficiency or low vision. The core problem is that relying on color alone makes it impossible for these users to perceive critical information about form requirements or errors. To implement this correctly, developers must ensure that required fields or errors are indicated using non-color methods, such as text labels, icons, borders, or changes in presentation (like bolding or increased contrast). This failure condition relates directly to Success Criterion 1.4.1 (Use of Color), ensuring that color is not the sole means of conveying essential information.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure of visually formatting input fields without providing necessary textual context, ensuring accessibility for users with visual or cognitive disabilities. The core problem is that visual patterns alone are insufficient for identifying complex data like phone numbers; explicit labels are required for full comprehension. To implement this fix, developers must ensure that any set of fields formatted to resemble a specific pattern (like parentheses and dashes) includes a visible text label clearly identifying the entire group as a "phone number." This failure condition relates directly to Success Criterion 3.3.2, which mandates that labels or instructions must be provided for form elements.

items.summary: This technique addresses failures in readability that occur when text is placed over background images lacking sufficient contrast. The core problem is that low vision users cannot accurately read text if the contrast between the foreground text and its background is too low, causing features of the image to interfere with recognition. To implement this successfully, ensure there is adequate contrast between the text and the specific area of the background it overlays. This requirement must be met for both minimum (1.4.3 Contrast) and enhanced (1.4.6 Contrast) contrast levels.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure of links that use non-specific text, such as "click here" or "more," which fail to communicate their destination purpose to users relying on assistive technologies like screen readers. The problem is that these vague links make navigation confusing for blind users who rely on reading link text alone to understand where they are going. To implement this fix, ensure all links have descriptive text that clearly indicates the content of the destination, or provide a mechanism (like an expandable button) to reveal more specific link text. This failure specifically relates to WCAG Success Criterion 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only).

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure condition where embedded dialogs or menus disrupt the sequential navigation order for keyboard users. The core problem is that if a dialog is opened without properly managing focus, keyboard users cannot easily interact with the interface because it is not positioned correctly in the tab sequence. To implement this successfully, developers must ensure that when a dialog opens, focus is immediately moved to it, and upon dismissal, focus is returned logically to the control that triggered the action. This ensures that the flow of keyboard navigation remains predictable throughout the user experience. The failure condition specifically relates to Success Criterion 2.4.3 regarding Focus Order.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure condition where multi-part form fields, such as those for a telephone number, lack proper naming for each individual component. The problem is that without distinct names, assistive technologies cannot correctly identify and label every input field, leading to confusion for users relying on screen readers or other assistive tools. To implement this successfully, ensure that every subfield within the multi-part form has a unique, programmatically determined name associated with it (e.g., using `id` attributes and proper `<label>` associations). This ensures that each part of the input is clearly defined, preventing ambiguity for users with disabilities. It directly relates to Success Criterion 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value).

These gaps make the text difficult for users with cognitive disabilities to read and process. To avoid this issue, content should never be fully justified across the entire line. Instead, use left-aligned or right-aligned text layouts for better readability. This failure relates directly to Success Criterion 1.4.8 regarding Visual Presentation.

items.summary: This technique addresses failures where removing focus from a form element causes an unintended change in context or behavior. The core problem is ensuring that sequential interaction with form fields does not trigger unwanted actions, such as automatic submission, navigation, or the opening of new windows. items.summary: This technique addresses failures in correctly associating table headers and content using the `id` and `headers` attributes. It solves the problem where the programmatic relationship between data cells (`<td>`) and their corresponding header cells (`<th>`) cannot be determined accurately, often occurring in complex or nested tables. To implement this successfully, authors must ensure that the `headers` attribute in data cells correctly references the specific IDs of the relevant header cells. This failure condition directly relates to Success Criterion 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships), ensuring that the structure of the table accurately reflects the relationships between its elements.

items.summary: This technique addresses the failure condition where HTML5 media elements automatically begin playback without providing users with a means to pause or stop the content. The core problem is that unmanaged autoplay can be disruptive and frustrating for the user experience. To avoid this failure, developers must ensure that if an `audio` or `video` element uses the `autoplay` attribute, controls are provided that allow the user to halt playback. This ensures that users maintain control over media consumption rather than being subjected to continuous, unwanted playback. The technique relates directly to Success Criterion 1.4.2 (Audio Control), emphasizing the need for proper management of media playback.

items.summary: This technique documents a failure condition related to text resizing when viewport units are used for font sizing. The core problem is that using units like `vw` or `vh` makes the text size relative to the viewport, preventing standard browser controls (like zooming or text-sizing features) from effectively adjusting the text size. This failure occurs because viewport units prevent the text from scaling as expected according to accessibility guidelines. To implement this test, use CSS viewport units directly on the `font-size` property for text elements. This technique relates specifically to Success Criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text.

To implement this test, ensure that any content appearing on hover remains visible and movable without disappearing, allowing users to fully perceive and interact with the information. This failure relates directly to Success Criterion 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus).

This failure occurs when techniques like `aria-label` or hidden text introduce context that causes the accessible name to differ from the visible label string. To resolve this, developers must ensure that the accessible name contains at least a match for the visible label text so that screen readers and speech input can successfully associate the control with its intended purpose. Implementation involves carefully managing attributes like `aria-label` or using `aria-labelledby` to compose meaningful names based on visible content. This failure occurs when techniques like `aria-label` or hidden text introduce context that causes the accessible name to differ from the visible label string. To resolve this, developers must ensure that the accessible name contains at least a match for the visible label text so that screen readers and speech input can successfully associate the control with its intended purpose. Implementation involves carefully managing attributes like `aria-label` or using `aria-labelledby` to compose meaningful names based on visible content. This technique relates directly to Success Criterion 2.5.3 Label in Name (A).

items.summary: This technique addresses failures that occur when content is locked into a single landscape or portrait orientation, restricting user flexibility. The primary problem solved is ensuring that users are not unfairly limited in how they view content, especially for users with fixed viewing setups. To implement this test, check if the content allows for flexible orientation changes and verify whether the imposed orientation is truly essential for the content's operation or viewing. This failure condition relates directly to Success Criterion 1.3.4 Orientation (AA), ensuring that content can be viewed across multiple device orientations.

It mandates providing definitions for words used in a restricted, archaic, jargon, or idiomatic manner, thereby preventing misinterpretation. To implement it, content creators must review text and define any term that requires specific contextual understanding, such as technical jargon or regional idioms. This technique relates primarily to WCAG Success Criterion 3.1.3 (Sensory Characteristics) by ensuring that non-standard language is clearly communicated.

items.summary: Technique G103 addresses the challenge of making complex textual information accessible to users with reading disabilities by providing visual illustrations, pictures, and symbols. This technique helps users understand difficult concepts, processes, data, and events that are described in text through non-textual aids like charts, diagrams, flowcharts, and animations. To implement this effectively, content creators should use visuals to clarify relationships between ideas or illustrate step-by-step processes. Crucially, all visual materials must include appropriate text alternatives so that screen readers can convey the information to users who cannot perceive the images. This technique relates directly to Success Criterion 1.1.1, which requires non-text content to have text alternatives.

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of data loss that occurs when web sessions time out due to user inactivity, forcing a re-authentication. It solves this by allowing the server to temporarily cache sensitive form data while the user is logging in. Upon successful re-authentication, the cached data is restored, ensuring the user can complete the original task without losing entered information. Implementation involves configuring the web server to retain session data briefly after timeout for processing. This technique ensures data integrity and provides a seamless user experience during mandatory security checks. It relates primarily to session management and authentication controls (AAA).

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of unpredictable context changes that can confuse users with cognitive disabilities or those relying on assistive technologies like screen readers. It ensures that critical actions, such as opening a new window or navigating to the next screen, are triggered only by explicit user interactions rather than passive focus events. To implement this, developers should use interactive elements (like buttons) to trigger context changes instead of relying on `onfocus` events for these actions. This makes the flow of the application predictable and easier for all users to navigate. While not directly tied to a single WCAG success criterion, it strongly supports principles related to operability and predictability.

items.summary: Technique G108 addresses the need for assistive technologies (AT) to understand web content so that users can effectively interact with controls. It solves the problem of inaccessible user interfaces by ensuring that essential information about UI components is exposed. To implement this technique, authors must use standard markup features to explicitly define the name, role, and user-settable properties of each component. This relies on using documented attributes (like `name` or `role`) to provide necessary context for AT. Ultimately, G108 ensures that controls are operable and perceivable by making their functionality clear to assistive technologies.

items.summary: This technique addresses the issue of visual distraction caused by blinking content, which can be particularly challenging for users with learning disabilities or low vision. The goal is to minimize this distraction by limiting the duration of any blinking content to a maximum of five seconds. To implement this, developers should ensure that any animated elements, such as sale tags, stop blinking promptly after this short interval. This practice helps users re-focus on the main content without being overwhelmed by rapid visual changes. The technique directly relates to the Success Criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A).

items.summary: This technique addresses the need to implement redirects on the client side when server-side control is unavailable or impractical, aiming to provide an instant navigation experience without confusing the user. It allows authors to execute redirects using code within the content, such as HTML meta elements, instructing the user agent to retrieve content from a different URI. For effective implementation, the redirecting page should contain only information directly related to the redirection itself. Testing involves checking links for client-side redirects and ensuring these redirects are immediate and self-contained. This technique relates generally to content delivery and manipulation, falling under the broader category of AAA (Change on Request).

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of relying solely on color to convey critical information, which can exclude users with color vision deficiencies or low vision. To implement this effectively, whenever color differences are used to distinguish elements in non-text content, you must also incorporate distinct patterns, shapes, or textures to ensure the information remains accessible regardless of the user's ability to perceive color. The goal is to provide redundant visual cues so that all necessary information is conveyed through multiple sensory channels. This practice ensures that visual data is not dependent on a single visual property. It relates directly to WCAG principles concerning perceivability and alternative ways to present information.

items.summary: This technique, G112, solves the problem of ambiguity or potential misinterpretation arising from the use of unusual, restricted, or specialized terminology within a document. It ensures that specific terms are clearly understood by providing immediate context-based definitions. Implementation involves embedding the definition directly into the text, either immediately preceding or following the word being defined, allowing the reader to understand the term as it is used. This method is crucial for technical specifications, legal documents, or specialized reports where precise meaning is paramount. G112 relates primarily to information clarity and presentation rather than specific security controls (SCs).

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of ensuring that the structure and meaning of web content are accurately communicated to user agents and assistive technologies. Instead of relying solely on visual presentation, it mandates the use of semantic elements to explicitly define the role of different content units, such as headings, paragraphs, or citations. Implementation involves using appropriate markup languages (like HTML) to mark up relationships between content, for example, using `a` for links or `blockquote` for quotations. This practice makes the structure perceivable and understandable to users, regardless of how the content is visually styled. It relates primarily to the principles of HTML structure and semantics.

items.summary: This technique addresses the problem of relying solely on visual presentation—such as changes in font face, size, or color—to convey essential information. It ensures that content remains accessible and understandable for all users, including those using assistive technologies like screen readers. To implement this, whenever text variations are used to communicate meaning, the actual information must also be explicitly stated elsewhere in the text. This can be achieved by adding inline descriptions, separate sections, or alternative textual explanations accompanying the visual changes. The technique directly relates to Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A), emphasizing that information conveyed visually must also be available through text.

items.summary: G120 is a technique designed to improve content accessibility by providing immediate pronunciation information for words or abbreviations. The primary problem it solves is ensuring that readers, particularly those unfamiliar with specific terminology or foreign languages, can correctly understand how a word is spoken within the context of the web page. To implement this technique, you must provide the pronunciation immediately following the word, typically enclosed in parentheses, at least upon its first occurrence. This method is most effective when dealing with abbreviations or terms that might have multiple pronunciations. G120 directly relates to Search Criteria 3.1.6 Pronunciation (AAA), aiming to enhance clarity and comprehension for all users.

items.summary: This technique addresses the need for users to easily access and understand the correct pronunciation of words within a digital environment. It solves the problem of presenting text without providing necessary phonetic context, ensuring accessibility for all users. Implementation involves linking specific words to external resources or internal pages that contain detailed pronunciation information, such as dictionary entries, International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) representations, or audio files. The procedure requires verifying that every instance of a word is linked and that these links accurately navigate to the relevant phonetic data. This technique relates primarily to content presentation standards and accessibility requirements related to linguistic information.

items.summary: The G123 technique addresses the issue of excessive, repetitive content by allowing users to bypass large sections of material quickly. It solves the problem of unnecessary scrolling when navigating through long lists, indexes, or repeated navigation blocks. Implementation involves adding a link at the very beginning of a block of repeated content that directs keyboard focus immediately to the end of that block. When activated, this link skips over the entire section, allowing users to jump directly to the subsequent content. This technique falls under the category of bypassing content blocks, specifically relating to SC 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (A).

It achieves this by providing a mechanism—such as a table of contents—that links directly to various sections within the page. Implementation involves adding these navigational links at the top of the page, ensuring each link corresponds to a specific section of the content. The procedure requires testing that activating these links successfully moves the user's focus to the intended content area. This technique primarily relates to accessibility standards concerning focus management and navigation, particularly ARIA principles.

items.summary: The G125 technique addresses the need for efficient navigation by ensuring users can easily locate related information within a web page. It solves the problem of information silos by making content interconnected through hyperlinks, which is a fundamental component of the World Wide Web. To implement this, you must include links within the content that direct users to relevant, related web pages. The testing procedure involves verifying that each link successfully leads to the intended related information. This technique directly relates to Success Criterion 2.4.5 Multiple Ways (AA), ensuring that information is accessible through various navigation paths.

items.summary: The G126 technique is designed to solve the problem of locating all other web pages within a specific set, aiding in site navigation and content discovery. It involves scanning every page to identify and list links pointing to all other pages in the website. Implementation requires checking that each page contains a comprehensive list linking to every other page in the set. This technique is most effective for small sets of web pages. G126 directly relates to Success Criterion 2.4.5, which requires methods for locating multiple ways to access content.

It enables navigation and contextual awareness by explicitly linking a document to its parent structure. Implementation involves including identifying information—such as sub-site names, chapter numbers, or organizational titles—within the web page's title or metadata. This allows users to quickly identify the page's position within a larger set of documents. The technique relates to the structural requirements defined in SC 2.4.2 and 2.4.8.

items.summary: This technique addresses the risk of unexpected context changes when a user interacts with form controls or settings. It solves the problem of providing insufficient information, ensuring users are aware of the consequences before they trigger a change in application state. To implement this, authors must provide clear instructions or warnings that explicitly describe what will happen when a specific input or setting change results in a context shift. This is best achieved by placing these explanations logically preceding the control that causes the context change. By proactively informing the user, this technique mitigates confusion and potential security risks associated with unintended state transitions. It relates to principles concerning secure design and proper labeling (SCs 3.2.2 and 3.3.2).

The primary problem solved is helping users navigate web content efficiently and understand the organization of the page. To implement this effectively, authors must use descriptive headings and ensure that the most important information is placed at the beginning of each heading to aid skimming. This practice allows users to quickly orient themselves and locate specific sections within the document. This guideline directly relates to Success Criterion 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels) of WCAG AA.

The primary problem it solves is the lack of clarity regarding the purpose of controls, which prevents users relying on screen readers or other assistive tools from effectively interacting with the interface. To implement this, developers must use appropriate technology-specific methods to provide descriptive labels for every control, ensuring these labels accurately reflect the component's function. This practice allows assistive technologies to correctly identify and communicate the purpose of the control to the user. It relates directly to Success Criteria 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels) and 3.3.2 (Labels or Instructions).

items.summary: This technique addresses accessibility concerns by mitigating the risk of users losing work when completing complex multipart forms. It solves the problem of time constraints that can disproportionately affect users with disabilities, allowing them flexibility in task completion. To implement this, include a checkbox on the first page of the form enabling users to request an additional session time limit, such as 15 minutes or an indefinite extension. This feature ensures that users are not rushed and have adequate time to focus and complete all required steps. While primarily an accessibility measure, it relates to general security principles by ensuring equitable access to digital services.

items.summary: The G139 technique addresses the problem of efficiently guiding users to input errors when data is rejected by a system. It allows applications to detect invalid user input—such as missing required fields or incorrect values—and provide immediate feedback. Implementation involves using server-side or client-side validation to detect errors, followed by displaying descriptive error messages that include direct links to the specific fields with problems. This mechanism enables users to quickly navigate to and correct the erroneous data without manual searching. The technique directly relates to Security Criteria 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 3.3.3 (Error Suggestion).

items.summary: This technique ensures that information conveyed through color differences is accessible to all users, particularly those with color vision deficiencies or who use screen readers. The primary problem solved is preventing reliance solely on color to communicate critical status or meaning, which can render content inaccessible. To implement this effectively, authors must always provide a textual alternative—such as labels, descriptive text, or icons—to accompany any use of color for conveying information. This ensures that the meaning remains clear regardless of the visual presentation. G14 directly relates to WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color.

items.summary: The G140 technique solves the problem of ensuring that content structure is explicitly communicated to assistive technologies, which is often obscured by purely presentational formatting. It achieves this by logically separating the structural encoding (headings, lists, paragraphs) from the presentational encoding (color, font size). Implementation involves using reserved technology features for structure and applying styling rules separately, allowing user agents to understand the content's semantic organization regardless of visual presentation. This separation enables assistive technologies to perform meaningful transformations on the content, such as reordering sections or interacting with list items based on their structural characteristics. While not directly tied to a specific SC, this technique is fundamental to achieving semantic structure and accessibility goals within WCAG principles.

items.summary: This technique solves the problem of organizing content into a logical, navigable structure by ensuring that sections are clearly identified. To implement this, authors should use HTML heading elements (`h1` through `h6`) to mark these sections. It is crucial that these headings are properly nested (e.g., an `h2` must follow an `h1`, and subsequent headings must follow a logical hierarchy) to facilitate understanding of the document structure. This practice directly supports Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, which requires content to be programmatically identifiable.

items.summary: This technique addresses the accessibility requirement that content must be scalable and uniformly readable by users who adjust text size or zoom their display. The goal is to ensure that the layout and functionality of the content remain intact when viewed through user agents that support zooming capabilities. Implementation involves ensuring that the HTML and CSS structure are inherently responsive, allowing the browser's built-in zoom functions to scale all elements proportionally. It is critical that this scaling preserves all spatial relationships and ensures that all interactive features remain fully accessible and functional. This technique directly relates to WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.4 (Resize text).
